title: 1 Kings 9:15–28
context: This section gathers notices about Solomon’s building program and administration. It explains the forced labor he conscripted for the temple, the palace, the Millo, Jerusalem’s wall and the cities of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. It records that Pharaoh had captured Gezer and given it as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon’s wife. It lists other building projects and states that the remaining Canaanite peoples were made bondservants, while Israelites served as soldiers and officials. Pharaoh’s daughter moves into her house, Solomon offers sacrifices three times a year, and he builds a fleet at Ezion Geber with Hiram’s sailors that brings gold from Ophir. The text reports these matters without stating motives. Readers have long noticed a tension with 5:13–14, where a levy is raised out of all Israel, and with 12:4, where the people complain of a heavy yoke. Some explain it by distinguishing permanent bond service for the Canaanites from temporary rotating labor for Israelites; others see different sources or emphases. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 8 differs in some numbers, such as 250 officers (2 Chronicles 8:10) where verse 23 has 550, and 450 talents (2 Chronicles 8:18) where verse 28 has 420. Both traditions read the section as narrative and description.

verses.text: This is the reason of the forced labor which King Solomon conscripted: to build the LORD’s house, his own house, Millo, Jerusalem’s wall, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
verses.arminianNotes:
The text gives the reason for the forced labor Solomon conscripted: to build the LORD’s house, his own house, the Millo, Jerusalem’s wall, and the cities of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. The Millo was probably a terrace or fill structure, though its exact nature is uncertain.

Arminian readers note that the verse reports the purpose of the labor without commending or condemning it, and readers should hold together the grandeur of the work with its human cost.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrative will later show the people describing Solomon’s demands as a heavy yoke (12:4), so the record of forced labor quietly contributes to the story of the kingdom’s division, without the text supplying a motive here.

Both traditions report the notice as the text gives it.

verses.text: Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up, taken Gezer, burned it with fire, killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and given it for a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon’s wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
Pharaoh king of Egypt had captured Gezer, burned it, killed its Canaanite inhabitants, and given it as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon’s wife. The marriage was mentioned at 3:1.

Arminian readers note that this alliance with Egypt is reported as political fact, and that the text does not here comment on its wisdom, though later chapters show Solomon’s foreign marriages drawing his heart away (11:1–4).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this Pharaoh is not named, and while scholars have proposed identifications, none is certain; Gezer itself is a well-known city on the route between the coast and Jerusalem.

Both traditions read the notice as historical background and avoid confident claims beyond the text.

verses.text: Solomon built in the land Gezer, Beth Horon the lower,
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon builds Gezer and lower Beth Horon. These sites guarded routes into the hill country.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s fortification of key towns reflects prudent stewardship of the kingdom’s security, a legitimate responsibility of a ruler that the text reports without criticism.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s gift of peace to Solomon (5:4) was accompanied by practical measures for defense, illustrating that God’s providence works through human planning and effort rather than replacing it.

Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of Solomon’s building program, without theological dispute.

verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon also builds Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:4 names Tadmor in the wilderness, and some translations read Tadmor here.

Arminian readers note that the identification of these places is uncertain, and that the list’s purpose is to show the extent of Solomon’s building activity rather than to provide a precise map.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that interpreters differ over whether Tamar in the south or Tadmor in the north is meant, and the difference need not be resolved with confidence to grasp the narrative’s point about the scope of Solomon’s projects.

Both traditions hold such geographical questions with humility.

verses.text: all the storage cities that Solomon had, the cities for his chariots, the cities for his horsemen, and that which Solomon desired to build for his pleasure in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon builds all his storage cities, chariot cities, cities for his horsemen, and whatever he desired to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon and throughout his dominion. The list is sweeping.

Arminian readers note that the phrase whatever he desired to build may hint at royal ambition, though the text does not pass judgment, and readers should weigh it alongside the later warnings about the king’s heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the mention of chariot and horsemen cities anticipates 10:26–29, where the accumulation of horses echoes the warning of Deuteronomy 17:16, though here the notice is simply descriptive.

Both traditions read the verse as description that later chapters will set in a larger moral context.

verses.text: As for all the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel—
verses.arminianNotes:
As for the people left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, who were not Israelites, the text now turns to them. These are the remaining peoples of the land.

Arminian readers note that the list recalls the peoples named in the conquest accounts, and that the continued presence of these peoples is a reminder of Israel’s incomplete obedience in earlier generations (Judges 1:27–36).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator connects Solomon’s administration with the long history of Israel and the nations in the land, so that his policies are framed as the outworking of that history rather than as an isolated decision.

Both traditions read the verse as historical narrative that sets up the notice in verse 21.

verses.text: their children who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel were not able utterly to destroy—of them Solomon raised a levy of bondservants to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Their descendants who remained in the land, whom Israel could not completely destroy, Solomon conscripted as bondservants to this day. The text records a permanent levy.

Arminian readers note that the verse reports the policy as the text gives it, and that modern readers rightly feel the weight of such forced labor while recognizing that the narrator is describing, not prescribing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase to this day reflects the narrator’s later vantage point, and that the account distinguishes this permanent bond service from the labor of Israelites mentioned elsewhere; how the two relate is debated.

Both traditions report the notice soberly, without supplying motives the text does not state.

verses.text: But of the children of Israel Solomon made no bondservants; but they were the men of war, his servants, his princes, his captains, and rulers of his chariots and of his horsemen.
verses.arminianNotes:
But Solomon made no Israelites bondservants; they served as soldiers, officials, commanders, and captains of his chariots and horsemen. This seems to contrast with 5:13–14.

Arminian readers note the apparent tension with the levy raised out of all Israel in 5:13–14 and the heavy yoke of 12:4; some distinguish permanent bond service from temporary rotating labor, while others see differing sources or emphases.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the distinction between Israelites and the remaining Canaanites reflects covenant identity, while the narrative elsewhere shows that Israel still felt the burden of Solomon’s demands; the text holds both without resolving every detail.

Both traditions acknowledge the tension honestly and hold the harmonization with humility.

verses.text: These were the five hundred fifty chief officers who were over Solomon’s work, who ruled over the people who labored in the work.
verses.arminianNotes:
These were the five hundred fifty chief officers over Solomon’s work, who ruled over the people who labored. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:10 has two hundred fifty.

Arminian readers note that some interpreters observe that 550 here plus 3,300 in 5:16 equals 250 in Chronicles plus 3,600 in 2 Chronicles 2:18, suggesting different ways of grouping the same officials, though this remains a proposal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that differences in numbers between Kings and Chronicles are handled in various ways, including different categories of officials or copying differences, and that the narrative point, an organized administration, is clear either way.

Both traditions hedge the numbers and avoid overconfident harmonization.

verses.text: But Pharaoh’s daughter came up out of David’s city to her house which Solomon had built for her. Then he built Millo.
verses.arminianNotes:
Pharaoh’s daughter comes up from David’s city to the house Solomon built for her, and then he builds the Millo. Her house had been mentioned at 7:8.

Arminian readers note that the narrator records the move as part of the building program, and that the honor given to this foreign wife will later be part of the story of how Solomon’s marriages affected his heart (11:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:11 gives a reason connected with the holiness of places where the ark had been, while Kings simply reports the move; the Chronicler’s reason is not read back into Kings without care.

Both traditions read the verse as historical narrative.

verses.text: Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar which he built to the LORD three times per year, burning incense with them on the altar that was before the LORD. So he finished the house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Three times a year Solomon offers burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he built for the LORD, burning incense before the LORD, and so he finishes the house. The pattern likely corresponds to the three annual festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16).

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s regular worship shows genuine devotion at this stage, and that faithful worship must be sustained over time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the notice affirms Solomon’s proper worship at the central sanctuary, in contrast to the high places mentioned earlier (3:2–3), and that worship is the proper end of the temple’s construction.

Both traditions see Solomon’s worship here as fitting and good, while knowing that his later turning makes this a high point.

verses.text: King Solomon made a fleet of ships in Ezion Geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.
verses.arminianNotes:
King Solomon builds a fleet of ships at Ezion Geber, near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea in Edom. This port is generally placed at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba, though its exact site is debated.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s maritime venture shows his initiative in expanding trade, an exercise of the wisdom and opportunity God had given him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reference to Edom reflects the extent of the territory under Solomon’s control, in keeping with the promises of land and dominion given to Israel, though the text simply records the fact. The Hebrew name for this sea is the same one used at the exodus.

Both traditions read the verse as historical description.

verses.text: Hiram sent in the fleet his servants, sailors who had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram sends his servants, experienced sailors, with Solomon’s servants in the fleet. Tyre was known for seafaring.

Arminian readers note that the partnership with Hiram’s sailors illustrates how Solomon’s kingdom benefited from the skills of other nations, and that cooperation with outsiders is not in itself a compromise of faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s blessing on Solomon included the expertise of foreign allies, showing that God uses the gifts he has given to all peoples for his purposes, as he did in the building of the temple (5:6).

Both traditions read the verse as a positive notice of cooperation.

verses.text: They came to Ophir, and fetched from there gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to King Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
They go to Ophir and bring back four hundred twenty talents of gold to King Solomon. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:18 has four hundred fifty talents.

Arminian readers note that the location of Ophir is unknown, with proposals including Arabia, East Africa and India, and that the narrative’s emphasis is on the great wealth that flowed to Solomon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that differences between the figures in Kings and Chronicles need not be resolved with certainty, and that both accounts agree on the main point of extraordinary wealth, which the following chapter will both celebrate and quietly question.

Both traditions hedge the numbers and the geography.
